title: Barbershop
full_review:
"The cornerstone of the community" is how one character describes the local haircutting establishment in the enjoyable ensemble comedy "Barbershop" (MGM).

Set over the course of a day in Chicago's South Side, director Tim Story's film focuses on the importance of a local tonsorial parlor in an African-American neighborhood as a gathering place where more than just haircuts are given. The movie is flawed by silly stereotypes and predictability, yet manages to be endearing as it touches on racism, fellowship and the black man's place in society.

A hub of conversation and gossip as well as a safe haven for free speech, the barbershop hosts spontaneous discussions on everything from reparation, the guilt or innocence of O.J. Simpson and the beauty of a certain female body part. Inheriting the barbershop from his father, Calvin (Ice Cube) is more interested in get-rich schemes (from herbal franchises to a do-it-yourself recording studio in his basement) than running the shop.

Already deep in debt, he decides to sell the store to sinister loan shark and local gangster Lester (Keith David), who is only missing a twirling mustache to go with his powder-blue suit and derby to more clearly indicate him as the dastardly villain. But when Calvin learns that Lester plans to turn the shop into a strip joint, turning the haircutters out into the street, he realizes his mistake and must somehow convince Lester to call off the deal.

The barbershop's motley crew includes old-timer Eddie (Cedric the Entertainer in a graying, Al Sharpton-like wig), the group's loud-mouthed historian with strong opinions and no customers. Pretentious latte-sipping Jimmy (Sean Patrick Thomas), who wears his superiority complex like a merit badge, is constantly sparring with Isaac (Troy Garity), a white barber who just wants a chance to prove he can cut hair with the best of them in the 'hood. Ricky (Michael Ealy) is an ex-con with two strikes against him who's trying to stay straight and out of the way of Terri (rap star Eve), the only female hair clipper, who can't get over her addiction to her two-timing boyfriend or get people to leave her apple juice alone.

A sideline story that eventually ties into the main narrative involves the theft of an automated-teller machine by a pair of bungling burglars (Anthony Anderson and Lahmard Tate) that plays like a poor man's Abbott and Costello slapstick scene. Although the humor sometimes dips into the arena of sexual suggestiveness, it stays above puerile toilet humor, succeeding in garnering a few laughs. The script allows for plenty of ad-libbing from the actors, who bounce off one another in the convincing, natural manner of people who have long been in each other's faces.

"Barbershop" is a pleasant surprise that, while mainly superficial in its treatment of heavy subjects, entertains with an underlying tenderness for the local community hangouts that have been replaced by more impersonal places like Starbuck's.

Due to some sexual innuendo, fleeting drug content and sporadic crass expressions and profanity with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
